state.case_summary:
A 47-year-old Caucasian woman with a 23-year history of presumed multiple sclerosis—characterized by four episodes of optic neuritis since 1989, a longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis in 1995, persistently negative cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) oligoclonal bands, and unremarkable brain MRI scans—was treated with monthly intravenous methylprednisolone pulses and interferon-β. In January 2012, she presented with subacute onset of expressive aphasia and right-sided hemiparesis. On examination, she was alert with expressive language impairment and 3/5 strength in the right arm and leg; vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies demonstrated a normal complete blood count and metabolic panel. Brain MRI showed a large T2-hyperintense, tumefactive lesion in the left prefrontal white matter and smaller T2 lesions on the right without clear evidence of a disturbed blood–brain barrier. MR spectroscopy revealed an unchanged choline peak. CSF analysis was unremarkable, with no evidence of intrathecal immunoglobulin synthesis, no oligoclonal bands, and a normal cell count. Time-of-flight MR angiography showed no signs of vasculitis, and laboratory work-up revealed no clinical or serological evidence for connective tissue diseases. Serum aquaporin-4 antibody titre was 1:1000 by cell-based assay.
